title: Ensemble Methods
blurb: Tests why combining models works: bagging and Random Forests for variance, boosting for bias, and stacking with out-of-fold predictions. Includes hand calculations of correlated-average variance, bootstrap coverage, majority votes and gradient-boosting updates.

ideas.title: Why ensembles work: diverse errors and correlation

refLinks.label: §12.2.2 Random Forests — Bagging Plus Feature Randomness

ideas.title: Boosting and gradient boosting by hand
XGBoost, LightGBM and choosing a first ensemble

questions.prompt: Averaging many models beats a single model only under one condition. Which?
options: Each model must be more accurate than the best single model
The models must make different errors, so their mistakes cancel
There must be at least 100 models in the ensemble
The models must all be the same algorithm with the same settings
questions.explanation: The gain comes from diversity of errors. If every model fails on the same examples, averaging changes nothing. The base models can be weak, which is the point of the wisdom-of-crowds idea. Identical models trained on identical data make identical errors, so they give no gain at all.

questions.prompt: In bagging, how is each model's bootstrap sample built from a training set of $n$ rows?
options: Draw $n$ rows with replacement, so some rows repeat and some are left out
Draw $n$ rows without replacement, so each row appears once in a new order
Draw the rows the previous model got wrong, with extra weight
Split the rows into $B$ disjoint chunks, one chunk per model
questions.explanation: Each draw puts the row back before the next draw. So a bootstrap sample of size $n$ has repeats and misses some rows. Drawing without replacement would give every model the same data in a new order, which gives no diversity. Reweighting the previous model's mistakes is boosting, not bagging.

questions.prompt: What does a Random Forest add on top of plain bagged trees, and why?
options: Every tree is pruned back to depth 4, which cuts the variance of each tree
A meta-learner weights the trees, which lets the strongest trees count more
Each tree is trained on the previous tree's residuals, which reduces bias
Each split considers a random subset of features, which decorrelates the trees
questions.explanation: Without feature randomness most bagged trees pick the same dominant feature at the root, so they are correlated and their errors do not cancel. Considering roughly $\sqrt{p}$ features at each split forces the trees apart. Training on residuals is gradient boosting. A learned weighting of models is stacking. Random Forests usually grow trees to full depth.

refLinks.label: §12.2.2 Random Forests — Bagging Plus Feature Randomness

questions.prompt: How does boosting differ from bagging?
options: Boosting trains models in parallel on bootstrap samples and mainly cuts variance
Boosting trains models in sequence on random feature subsets, and mainly cuts noise
Boosting trains one very deep tree and then prunes it back, and mainly cuts variance
Boosting trains models in sequence, each fixing earlier mistakes, and mainly cuts bias
questions.explanation: Boosting is sequential. AdaBoost reweights misclassified rows, gradient boosting fits each new tree to the current residuals. Either way, each learner fixes what the ensemble still gets wrong, which reduces bias. Parallel training on bootstrap samples is bagging, which reduces variance. No method removes irreducible noise.

questions.prompt: Which technique is LightGBM's own speed idea, as the chapter describes it?
options: Growing each tree level by level, then pruning it back later
Growing trees leaf-wise, splitting the leaf that cuts loss most
Averaging a stack of base models with a Ridge meta-learner
Training every tree on its own bootstrap sample in parallel
questions.explanation: LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise, splitting the leaf with the largest loss reduction wherever it sits. It adds Gradient-based One-Side Sampling and Exclusive Feature Bundling. Growing then pruning back is how the chapter describes XGBoost. Parallel bootstrap trees are bagging, and a Ridge meta-learner is stacking.

questions.prompt: In stacking, what data is the meta-learner trained on?
options: The raw training features, with the true labels as targets
The base models' predictions on the rows they were trained on
The base models' out-of-fold predictions, against the true labels
The base models' predictions on the held-out test set rows
questions.explanation: Each base model's predictions come from cross-validation, so every row is predicted by a model that did not see it. Those out-of-fold predictions become the meta-learner's features. In-sample predictions leak, because a flexible base model looks near-perfect on rows it memorised. Training the meta-learner on test predictions would leak the test set.

questions.prompt: How is permutation importance computed for a feature?
options: Sum the impurity reduction at every split that uses the feature
Shuffle the feature's values and measure the drop in score
Retrain the model without the feature and count the extra trees needed
Read the feature's coefficient from a stacked meta-learner
questions.explanation: Permutation importance breaks the link between one feature and the target by shuffling it, then measures the drop in score. It is slower but not biased toward high-cardinality features. Summing impurity reduction is what `.feature_importances_` does, and that is the version biased toward high-cardinality features.

questions.prompt: Five classifiers each have accuracy 0.70 and make independent errors. The ensemble predicts by majority vote. What is the probability that the vote is correct? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: The vote is right when at least 3 of 5 are right. With $X \sim \text{Binomial}(5, 0.7)$: $P(X=3) = 10 \times 0.343 \times 0.09 = 0.3087$, $P(X=4) = 5 \times 0.2401 \times 0.3 = 0.3602$, $P(X=5) = 0.1681$. Sum: 0.837. Independence is doing all the work here. If the five models made the same errors, the vote would stay at 0.70.

questions.prompt: A training set has 1,000 rows. A bootstrap sample draws 1,000 rows with replacement. The chance that a given row is never drawn is $(1 - 1/1000)^{1000}$. What is the expected number of **distinct** original rows in one bootstrap sample? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: $(1 - 0.001)^{1000} = 0.3677$, close to $1/e = 0.368$. So each row is included with probability $1 - 0.3677 = 0.6323$, and the expected number of distinct rows is $1000 \times 0.6323 = 632$. The other 368 slots are repeats. Answering 1,000 forgets that sampling with replacement produces duplicates.

questions.prompt: A `RandomForestClassifier` is trained on 50 features with `max_features='sqrt'`. scikit-learn rounds $\sqrt{p}$ down to an integer. How many features does each split consider? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{50} = 7.07$, rounded down to 7. Every split in every tree draws a fresh random set of 7 of the 50 features and picks the best split among them. A common slip is thinking the 7 are chosen once per tree. They are redrawn at each split.

questions.prompt: Gradient boosting for squared error starts from the mean of $y$. Three training rows have targets $y = (3, 5, 10)$. The first tree is a stump that puts rows 1 and 2 in one leaf and row 3 in another. Each leaf predicts the mean residual of its rows. The learning rate is 0.1. What is the ensemble's prediction for row 3 after this first tree? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation: Start: $F_0 = (3+5+10)/3 = 6$ for every row. Residuals: $(-3, -1, 4)$. Leaves: rows 1–2 predict $(-3-1)/2 = -2$, row 3 predicts 4. Update: $F_1 = F_0 + 0.1 \times \text{leaf}$, so row 3 gets $6 + 0.4 = 6.4$. Forgetting the learning rate gives 10.0, a full correction in one step, which is the aggressive behaviour shrinkage exists to prevent.

refLinks.label: §12.2.4 Gradient Boosting — Boosting as Gradient Descent

questions.prompt: A logistics customer has 30 million rows of tabular shipment data, many missing values, and retrains nightly in a tight window. Following Procedure 12.3, what is the first ensemble to try?
options: Random Forest, because it needs almost no tuning to work well
A stack of five models, because it squeezes out the last percent
Plain bagging of deep trees, because it removes the bias
LightGBM, since it trains fast at scale and handles missing values
questions.explanation: Two of Procedure 12.3's triggers fire: training speed is critical on a large dataset, and missing values are present. LightGBM covers both. Random Forest is the pick when there is no time to tune, but it is slower here and does not reduce bias the way boosting does. Stacking is not a default. Bagging reduces variance, not bias.

questions.prompt: A Ridge meta-learner in a house-price stack has intercept 5,000 and weights 1.15 on LightGBM and −0.12 on Random Forest. For one house, LightGBM predicts 320,000 dollars and Random Forest predicts 300,000 dollars. What does the stack predict, in dollars? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: $5000 + 1.15 \times 320000 + (-0.12) \times 300000 = 5000 + 368000 - 36000 = 337000$. The negative weight means the meta-learner partly subtracts Random Forest's prediction. It is not a weighted average, so the result can fall outside the range of the base predictions.

questions.prompt: A house-price model has test RMSE 28.0 (thousand dollars). With `n_repeats=3`, shuffling `sqft` gives test RMSE 40.1, 41.3 and 39.8. What is the permutation importance of `sqft`, measured as the mean increase in RMSE, in thousand dollars? Give a decimal to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation: Mean shuffled RMSE: $(40.1 + 41.3 + 39.8)/3 = 40.4$. Increase: $40.4 - 28.0 = 12.4$. Repeating the shuffle averages out the luck of one permutation, which is why Listing 12.2 uses `n_repeats=10`.

questions.prompt: Each tree in a forest has prediction variance $\sigma^2$, and every pair of trees has correlation $\rho = 0.25$. The variance of the average of $n$ trees is $\rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{n}\sigma^2$. What is the smallest $n$ that brings the ensemble variance below $0.27\sigma^2$? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: Need $0.25 + 0.75/n < 0.27$, so $0.75/n < 0.02$ and $n > 37.5$. The answer is 38. Note the floor. However many trees you add, the variance never drops below $\rho\sigma^2 = 0.25\sigma^2$. With $\rho = 0$ the formula becomes the chapter's $\sigma^2/B$. Lowering $\rho$, which is what feature randomness does, is the only way past the floor.

refLinks.label: §12.2.2 Random Forests — Bagging Plus Feature Randomness

questions.prompt: A customer bagged 500 ordinary linear regressions on 50,000 rows. Validation RMSE is the same as one linear regression, and train and validation RMSE are both high and close together. Why did bagging not help?
options: 500 models is too few, because bagging needs thousands to show a gain
Bagging raised the bias, cancelling out its variance reduction
Linear regression cannot be trained on bootstrap samples
The problem is bias, and bagging only reduces variance
questions.explanation: Train and validation errors both high and close is the high-bias pattern. A linear regression on 50,000 rows is already stable, so averaging 500 near-identical fits changes almost nothing. Bagging cuts variance and leaves bias unchanged. The fix is a more flexible model or boosting, which targets bias. That is why bagging pairs with high-variance learners such as deep trees.

questions.prompt: A dataset has 25 features, and one of them, `tenure`, is far stronger than the rest. A Random Forest of 200 trees uses 5 randomly chosen candidate features at each split. In how many trees, in expectation, is `tenure` **not** among the candidates at the root split? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: The chance `tenure` is in the 5 candidates is $5/25 = 0.2$, so it is missing with probability $0.8$. Expected trees: $200 \times 0.8 = 160$. In plain bagging every tree could use `tenure` at the root, so the trees look alike and are correlated. Here 80% of trees must start from another feature, which is how feature randomness decorrelates the forest.

refLinks.label: §12.2.2 Random Forests — Bagging Plus Feature Randomness

questions.prompt: Continue the example: $y = (3, 5, 10)$, $F_0 = 6$, learning rate 0.1. After the first stump, predictions are $F_1 = (5.8, 5.8, 6.4)$. The second tree uses the same split (rows 1 and 2 together, row 3 alone) and each leaf predicts the mean residual of its rows. What is $F_2$ for row 3? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation: New residuals: $y - F_1 = (-2.8, -0.8, 3.6)$. Leaf for row 3: 3.6. Leaf for rows 1–2: $(-2.8-0.8)/2 = -1.8$. Update row 3: $6.4 + 0.1 \times 3.6 = 6.76$. Each tree fits what is left over, so the residual on row 3 shrinks by a factor 0.9 each round (4, 3.6, 3.24). A common slip is to refit the original residual 4, which gives 6.8.

refLinks.label: §12.2.4 Gradient Boosting — Boosting as Gradient Descent

questions.prompt: A customer's XGBoost model uses `learning_rate=0.3`, `max_depth=10` and `n_estimators=1000`. Training RMSE is near zero. Validation RMSE bottoms out around round 120 and then rises. Which change follows the chapter's guidance?
options: Use `max_depth` 4 and `learning_rate` 0.05, tuning the tree count by CV
Keep the settings and add a Ridge stack on top to fix the overfit
Raise `learning_rate` to 0.5 so it converges before overfitting
Switch to a Random Forest with `n_estimators=5000` to cut bias
questions.explanation: The Trade-offs table names this exact risk. Gradient boosting overfits if trees are too deep or the learning rate too high. Procedure 12.1 suggests `max_depth=4` and a smaller learning rate (0.05) with more trees, chosen by cross-validation. A higher learning rate makes each step more aggressive. More Random Forest trees do not reduce bias. Stacking does not repair an overfit base model.

questions.prompt:
Which line makes this stack leak?

```python
for name, model in base_models.items():
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)                    # line 2
    oof[name] = model.predict(X_train)             # line 3
    test_preds[name] = model.predict(X_test)       # line 4
meta = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(
    np.column_stack(list(oof.values())), y_train)  # line 5
```
options: Line 5, because Ridge needs `alpha=0` inside any stack
Line 2, because base models must never be fitted on `y_train`
Line 3, because the meta-features are in-sample predictions
Line 4, because test predictions must come from the meta-learner
questions.explanation: Line 3 predicts on the same rows the model was fitted to. Those predictions are far better than anything the model will produce on new data, so the meta-learner learns weights for a situation that never occurs at test time. The fix is `cross_val_predict(model, X_train, y_train, cv=kf)`, as in Listing 12.4. Fitting on the full training set in line 2 is correct for producing test predictions.

questions.prompt: A churn Random Forest's `.feature_importances_` ranks `zip_code` (4,000 distinct values) first. Permutation importance on the test set puts `zip_code` near zero and `tenure` first. What should you tell the customer?
options: Trust the impurity ranking. It uses every split, so it has more information.
Permutation importance is biased toward low-cardinality features, so average the two.
Both are wrong. Only a single retrained, fully grown tree gives a true ranking.
Impurity importance favours high-cardinality features. Let permutation break the tie.
questions.explanation: A feature with 4,000 values offers many possible split points, so trees use it often and its impurity total grows, even when those splits only fit noise. Permutation importance asks whether the test score drops when the feature is scrambled, and here it barely does. Procedure 12.2 says to use permutation importance as the tiebreaker when the two disagree.

questions.prompt: A team trains five gradient-boosted models on the same data and features with different random seeds. Each scores 0.70 accuracy, and they agree on 97% of test rows. They expect majority voting to reach about 0.84. What is the most realistic expectation?
options: Close to 0.70, because the models make nearly the same errors
About 0.84, because the binomial result holds for any five 0.70 models
Below 0.50, because correlated models cancel each other out
Above 0.90, because agreement means the models are confident
questions.explanation: The 0.837 figure assumes independent errors. Models that agree on 97% of rows are strongly correlated. Where they agree, the vote is the same as any single model. Only the 3% of disputed rows can change, so the vote stays close to 0.70. In the variance formula $\rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{n}\sigma^2$, a $\rho$ near 1 leaves almost all of $\sigma^2$. Correlation removes the gain. It does not reverse it.

refLinks.label: §12.2.2 Random Forests — Bagging Plus Feature Randomness

questions.prompt: In current scikit-learn, `RandomForestRegressor` defaults to `max_features=1.0` (all features), while `RandomForestClassifier` defaults to `'sqrt'`. A colleague runs `RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200)` on house prices. Select ALL statements that are true.
options: Setting `max_features` to a fraction such as 0.33 can decorrelate the trees
Decorrelating trees can raise each tree's own error while lowering the ensemble's error
Because the defaults differ, the √p rule from the chapter applies automatically to regression
Raising `n_estimators` to 2,000 will lower the variance floor set by tree correlation
With these defaults the regressor is bagged trees with no per-split feature randomness
questions.explanation: With all features available at each split, every tree sees the same candidates and only the bootstrap differs. That is plain bagging. More trees only shrink the $\frac{1-\rho}{n}\sigma^2$ term. The $\rho\sigma^2$ floor stays. Limiting candidate features lowers $\rho$. Each tree gets a little worse because it sometimes cannot use the best feature, but the average improves because errors cancel better. The √p rule applies only if you set it.

refLinks.label: §12.2.2 Random Forests — Bagging Plus Feature Randomness

questions.prompt: In a gradient-boosting run each new tree fits the current residual of a single-row leaf exactly, so each round multiplies that residual by $(1 - \eta)$, where $\eta$ is the learning rate. With $\eta = 0.3$ the residual falls below 5% of its starting value after 9 rounds. How many rounds does $\eta = 0.05$ need to fall below 5%? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: Need $0.95^k < 0.05$, so $k > \ln 0.05 / \ln 0.95 = 58.4$, giving $k = 59$. Check: $0.95^{58} = 0.051$, $0.95^{59} = 0.049$. For $\eta = 0.3$, $0.7^9 = 0.040$. So cutting the learning rate by a factor of 6 needs about 6.5 times as many trees. That is why Procedure 12.1 pairs a small learning rate (0.05) with 500–1,000 trees. The small steps cost trees but generalise better.

refLinks.label: §12.2.4 Gradient Boosting — Boosting as Gradient Descent

questions.prompt: A customer trains a meta-learner on each base model's predictions for its own training rows. They stack an unlimited-depth Random Forest and a `max_depth=4` LightGBM model. The meta-learner puts almost all its weight on the Random Forest, and test RMSE is worse than solo LightGBM. What best explains the weights?
options: Ridge always gives the larger weight to whichever base model is listed first
Deep trees nearly memorise training rows, so in-sample forest predictions look perfect
LightGBM's predictions were on a different scale, so Ridge shrank its weight
Random Forest is the stronger model on this data, and the meta-learner found that
questions.explanation: An unlimited-depth forest fits its own training rows far better than new rows. Its in-sample predictions track `y_train` closely, so a meta-learner trained on them trusts the forest. On test data the forest is much weaker, as the Worked Example shows (RMSE \$45,502 against \$28,323), so the stack loses to solo LightGBM. With out-of-fold predictions the meta-learner sees honest errors. In the chapter's run it then gave LightGBM 1.209 and Random Forest −0.184.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in your own words why bagging reduces variance without increasing bias, using the $\sigma^2/B$ relationship from this chapter's Exposition.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: If $B$ models each have variance $\sigma^2$ and their errors are uncorrelated, averaging them gives variance $\sigma^2/B$, strictly smaller as $B$ grows, with no term in that formula affecting bias. Bagging doesn't change what each individual model is trying to predict: no change to the systematic error, i.e. bias. It only reduces how much the ensemble's *average* prediction fluctuates around that target across different training samples.

bookExercises.prompt: State which of bagging or boosting each of the following targets: (a) a model that is systematically wrong on a specific subgroup of examples; (b) a model whose predictions change wildly with small changes to the training data.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) Boosting: a model systematically wrong on a subgroup has high bias on that subgroup, which boosting directly targets by reweighting/refitting on exactly the hard cases. (b) Bagging: wildly changing predictions from small training-data changes is the definition of high variance, which bagging's averaging over bootstrap samples is designed to reduce.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 12.5's setup, explain why Random Forest's RMSE barely changes between `n_estimators=200` and `n_estimators=500` (\$45,502 vs. \$45,514) while LightGBM's RMSE at the same two settings keeps improving slightly, from \$28,323 to \$28,159. What does this suggest about each method's sensitivity to over-provisioning trees?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Random Forest's RMSE barely moving from 200 to 500 trees (\$45,502 → \$45,514, marginally *worse*, well within noise) indicates bagging's variance reduction has already saturated before 200 trees: additional trees add averaging stability with diminishing, essentially flat returns. LightGBM keeps improving slightly over the same range (\$28,323 → \$28,159), because boosting is still reducing bias round by round at 200 trees. Each new tree is still correcting real signal the ensemble hasn't captured yet, not just fitting noise. That's the core asymmetry this chapter's Exposition draws between the two. Bagging's averaging effect plateaus once the ensemble is large enough to cancel variance. Boosting keeps extracting value from additional rounds for longer, up to the point, not yet reached here, where it starts overfitting instead.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 12.4 as a base, add XGBoost as a third base model to the stack. State, from this chapter's own measured numbers, whether you'd expect the resulting stack to beat solo XGBoost's \$28,873 RMSE.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: LightGBM, not XGBoost, is the single best individual model in this chapter's benchmark: \$28,323 RMSE, versus XGBoost's \$28,873. It's already one of the two models in the existing stack. That makes beating solo XGBoost's \$28,873 specifically a fairly low bar: LightGBM alone already clears it, so the three-model stack would need the meta-learner to badly mis-weight things for the combined prediction to land worse than \$28,873. The more interesting, harder bar is solo LightGBM's own \$28,323. This chapter's own measured result is a reason for caution there: the RF+LightGBM stack's meta-learner assigned Random Forest, the weaker base model, a *negative* weight, and the stack still ended up worse than solo LightGBM (\$29,535 vs. \$28,323). Adding XGBoost, weaker than LightGBM but stronger than Random Forest, could get down-weighted the same way and land close to solo LightGBM, or dilute it enough to land worse. Expect the three-model stack to beat solo XGBoost comfortably. Don't assume it beats solo LightGBM without checking.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer's data science team reports "we stacked five models and it's more accurate than any of them individually." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say before accepting that claim.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Which models were in the stack, and did you compare against the single best individual model before concluding the stack is better? This chapter's own measured result shows a stack can be worse than the best model it was built from, even with that model inside the stack. 'Stacked and improved over all five individually' needs to be checked against the best of the five, not just an average or the worst of them."

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague argues Random Forest should always be tried before XGBoost "because it's simpler." Using Procedure 12.3 and this chapter's measured accuracy gap (Random Forest's RMSE roughly 58% higher than XGBoost's), write the case for when that advice is right and when it isn't.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Random Forest-first is right when time-to-baseline matters more than squeezing out the last accuracy, since it needs almost no tuning and gives a solid, honest number quickly (per Procedure 12.3). It's the wrong default when the roughly 58% RMSE gap this chapter measured (Random Forest \$45,502 vs. XGBoost \$28,873) matters to the business outcome. At that point, the extra tuning effort XGBoost/LightGBM demand is worth paying for, and "simpler" shouldn't be conflated with "good enough."

bookExercises.prompt: Read the XGBoost paper's (Chen & Guestrin, 2016) abstract and introduction. Identify one engineering optimisation it describes that this chapter's Trade-offs section does not mention. Explain what problem it solves.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. Likely candidates include XGBoost's cache-aware block structure for out-of-core computation (enabling training on datasets larger than memory) or its weighted quantile sketch algorithm for approximate split-finding on weighted data. Either addresses a scalability problem (very large datasets, or weighted training samples) beyond what this chapter's Trade-offs table, which focuses on bias/variance/overfitting risk, covers.
